Choose one product to prepare for export first

Exporting means a buyer in another country receives your goods legally, in good condition, at a price that still pays you. The first decision is not the country. It is the **product**. A product that sells well in Ibadan may be a poor export because it is heavy for its price, spoils quickly, breaks in transit or falls under strict rules abroad. A small, light, stable product can travel well even from a home workshop.
A globe showing Africa and Europe
Before choosing a country, choose the product that can survive the journey and still make money.
Five tests for an export product

**Value per kilogram.** Freight is charged mostly by weight or size. A product worth a lot per kilogram (a hand-dyed adire scarf) carries freight easily. A cheap, heavy product (dried zobo leaves, raw shea nuts) needs sea freight and large volumes to make sense.

**Shelf life and stability.** Sea freight from Lagos to Europe and customs clearance can take weeks. A product must stay safe and attractive for the whole journey and then for months on a shop shelf. Dried, low-moisture goods (dried ginger, sesame, hibiscus calyces) travel better than fresh pepper or wet pastes.
**Fragility.** Glass jars and liquid soaps leak and break. Textiles and dried goods in sealed bags rarely do.

**Regulatory class.** Food, cosmetics and anything you swallow or put on skin face the strictest rules abroad. Crafts and textiles usually face fewer product rules, though labelling and customs rules still apply.

**Repeatable supply.** A buyer who likes your sample will ask for the same thing again, often in larger quantity. You must know where your raw materials come from and how much you can make per month without quality dropping.
Freight as a share of price

A quick way to compare products is to ask: if I sent one unit by air, what share of my local price would the freight eat? You need three numbers: the **gross weight** of one packed unit (product plus its packaging), an **air freight rate per kilogram** quoted by a forwarder or courier, and your **local selling price**. Divide the freight per unit by the price. A share above about half is a warning sign for air freight. It does not kill the product, but it tells you that product needs sea freight, bulk packing or a much higher foreign price.
Worked example: three products, one freight rate

For example, Funmi in Abeokuta makes a 250 g shea body cream in a glass jar (local price about N4,000), 1 kg bags of dried zobo leaves (about N3,000) and hand-dyed adire scarves (about N15,000). A forwarder has quoted her, for example, N8,000 per kg by air to London. All prices are approximate and only for practice.
She weighs one packed unit of each: the cream jar with lid and box weighs 0.40 kg, the zobo bag in its outer pouch 1.10 kg, the folded scarf in a sleeve 0.20 kg.
Freight per unit: cream 0.40 x 8,000 = N3,200; zobo 1.10 x 8,000 = N8,800; scarf 0.20 x 8,000 = N1,600.
Freight as a share of local price: cream 3,200 / 4,000 = 80%; zobo 8,800 / 3,000 = about 293%; scarf 1,600 / 15,000 = about 10.7%.

She then checks the other tests. The cream is a cosmetic in glass: fragile and, for the UK and EU, it needs a responsible person based in that market. The zobo is stable but very cheap per kg. The scarf is light, unbreakable and not a food or cosmetic.

Funmi chooses the adire scarf as her first export product. She keeps zobo as a later sea-freight product to sell in bulk with other producers, and decides the cream needs more groundwork before it can travel.

Shelf life you can prove

Buyers abroad will ask for your **shelf life** and how you know it. A guess is not enough. For dried foods, keep dated samples in their final packaging at room temperature and check them every month for smell, colour, insects and clumping. For anything regulated by NAFDAC, the shelf life on your registered label is the one to use. Write down what you observe. That written record is part of what makes you export ready.
Do not over-promise volume

A buyer may ask, 'Can you supply 2 tonnes a month?' Answer with the number you can actually make at the same quality, based on your last three months of production and your raw material supply. Promising more and failing on the second order damages trust far more than a smaller honest answer.
A simple capacity check

Look at your records for the last three months. How many units did you make in your best month and in your worst month? What stopped you making more: raw materials, drying space, hands, money or electricity? The worst month, not the best, is the safe number to offer a new export buyer. If you have no records, start counting now; the Simple Record-Keeping course on the WODDI Institute shows easy methods.

Finally, think about **who else** could help you reach volume. Many first exports from small producers happen when several women who make the same product to the same specification pack together under one name or through a cooperative. You will plan this in Module 3. For now, choose one product, not five. Export readiness is detailed work, and doing it well for one product teaches you the method for all the others.

Once you have a product, you need **one** first market. Trying to sell to 'the world' wastes data, money and time. You will look at three things for each possible country: is there demand for your product there, how hard are the product rules, and how easy and costly is it to get goods there and get paid.
Your product's customs name: the HS code

Every product crossing a border is classified with a number from the **Harmonized System (HS)**, maintained by the World Customs Organization. The first six digits are the same in every member country. Countries add more digits for their own tariff lines. Customs officers, freight forwarders, the trade-data tools below and the buyer's import duty all depend on this code, so getting it right is the first technical job.

Three kinds of buyers

**Diaspora shops and caterers** abroad already know products such as dried zobo, ogiri, ginger and adire. They buy small quantities and may accept a simple label, but they still must obey their country's import and labelling law. **Importers and distributors** buy larger volumes, ask for specifications, test reports and consistent supply, and often put your product on their customer list. **Online buyers** ordering one item at a time are possible for light products such as textiles and crafts, using courier services, but each parcel carries its own customs and delivery costs.

For food, two rules stand out. In the **EU and UK**, prepacked food must carry specific information in a language consumers there understand, and the 14 major allergens must be emphasised. In the **United States**, FDA requires food facilities that make, process, pack or hold food for US consumption to register, and requires **prior notice** to be submitted for imported food shipments. Inside **ECOWAS**, neighbouring markets such as Ghana are closer and cheaper by road, and the ECOWAS Trade Liberalisation Scheme exists for approved originating products. Ask NEPC whether your product qualifies before relying on it.
Scoring markets with weights

A **weighted scorecard** turns your research into a choice. Pick four or five criteria, give each a weight that adds up to 100%, score each country from 1 (poor) to 5 (good) and multiply. Score rule difficulty so that **easier** rules get a **higher** score, so that every high number is good.
Worked example: three markets for dried ginger

For example, Amina in Kaduna dries and packs ginger. She is choosing between the UK (diaspora shops), Ghana (wholesalers in Accra) and the USA. Her weights: demand 30%, ease of rules 25%, logistics cost 20%, buyer contacts 25%.
UK scores: demand 5, rules 2, logistics 2, contacts 4. Total = 0.30x5 + 0.25x2 + 0.20x2 + 0.25x4 = 1.5 + 0.5 + 0.4 + 1.0 = 3.40.
Ghana scores: demand 3, rules 4, logistics 5, contacts 3. Total = 0.9 + 1.0 + 1.0 + 0.75 = 3.65.
USA scores: demand 4, rules 2, logistics 1, contacts 3. Total = 1.2 + 0.5 + 0.2 + 0.75 = 2.65.
She checks the weights add up: 30 + 25 + 20 + 25 = 100%.
Ghana scores highest (3.65), so Amina prepares for Ghana first and keeps the UK (3.40) as her second market once her labels and test reports are ready.

An honest gap check

Export work is less forgiving than local trade. At home, a customer may accept a missing date or a bag that is slightly light. Abroad, a missing certificate can hold goods at the port while storage charges grow, or lead to the goods being refused and destroyed. The habit you need is **precision**: check every document, number and spelling against the buyer's instructions, twice.
Worked example: a gap check for dried ginger to Ghana
For example, Amina (from the last lesson) is preparing ginger for Accra wholesalers. She lists what she has and what she lacks.
Has: CAC business name registration, a business bank account, records of six months of production.
Lacks: NEPC exporter registration. Action: register online on the NEPC e-registration portal this month.
Unknown: whether the Ghanaian buyer needs a phytosanitary certificate and an ECOWAS certificate of origin. Action: ask the buyer by email and ask NEPC and NAQS which apply.
Lacks: a written product specification. Action: write one (Module 2, Lesson 1).
She counts: 3 items in place, 3 to close, 1 question to answer.
Amina's honest list shows four actions, each with an owner and a month. She now knows her real distance from a first shipment instead of guessing.
Money scams that target new exporters

Be very careful with any 'buyer' who promises a large order and then asks you to pay a fee first, for example for an import licence, a 'registration with our ministry', inspection, or a lawyer they choose. Real buyers do not ask suppliers to pay their import permits. Also beware of cheques or transfers for more than the invoice with a request to send back the difference. Verify the company (for UK companies you can search Companies House free online), speak by video call, and never send goods on credit to a first-time buyer you cannot verify.
Questions to put to your buyer in writing
Which documents will your customs and food or product authority ask for at import, and who issues each one?
Whose name and address must appear on the label and on the import documents?
Which Incoterm and named place do you prefer, and which port or airport will you use?
Do you need laboratory test reports, and for which tests?
How will you pay, and in which currency?

A written answer protects you. If a buyer later says a document was missing, you can show what they asked for. If a buyer cannot answer these basic questions about their own country, treat that as a warning sign and slow down.

Keep all your certificates in one folder, paper and scanned, with the expiry or renewal date written on the front page. When a buyer asks, you can send clear scans the same day. That speed and order is itself a signal that you are a serious exporter.

Agree numbers with the buyer

Limits such as maximum moisture or foreign matter differ between buyers and markets. Do not invent them. Ask the buyer for their specification, or for the standard they use, and copy their numbers into your sheet. If you cannot measure something yourself, name the laboratory you will use.
Lot numbers and retained samples

Give each production batch a **lot number**, for example HB-2611-03 meaning hibiscus, November 2026, third batch. Print it on every bag and carton. Keep a **retained sample** of each lot, around 200 g in a sealed, labelled bag, stored like the product, until well after the buyer has sold it. If a complaint arrives months later, you can open the retained sample and see whether the fault started with you or happened later in transit or storage.
Checking that bags are not under weight

Weight problems are one of the fastest ways to lose an importer. Use a digital scale that you check against a known weight, and weigh a random sample from each lot before packing cartons. Record every weight. Look at both the **average** and the **lowest** bag.
Worked example: ten bags from one lot
For example, Hauwa in Kano packs 1 kg bags of dried hibiscus for an importer whose rule is simple: no bag may be below 1,000 g net.
She picks 10 bags at random and weighs the contents: 1,012, 1,005, 998, 1,020, 1,008, 1,003, 1,015, 996, 1,010 and 1,007 g.
Total = 10,074 g, so the average = 10,074 / 10 = 1,007.4 g. The average looks fine.
But the lowest bag is 996 g and another is 998 g. Two of ten bags break the buyer's rule.
She raises her filling target to 1,010 g, re-checks every bag in the lot, tops up the light ones, and records the change.
The average alone would have hidden the problem. By checking the lowest weight, Hauwa fixed the lot before it left her store, at the cost of about 10 g extra per bag.

Pick sample bags from different points of the lot: the start, middle and end of packing, and from different drying trays or sacks. A sample taken only from the top of one sack can hide problems elsewhere. Write the date, lot number, who weighed and each weight in a lot record book, and keep it with the order file.
The export order process

An export order follows a predictable path. Writing it as a **standard operating procedure (SOP)** means you, or a helper, can follow it without forgetting a step. Each stage produces a document or a decision you keep in the order file.
One export order, start to finish
Enquiry and spec agreed
Sample sent and approved
Proforma invoice and payment terms
Production, checks, lot records
Documents and booking
Shipment, then payment confirmed
Nothing moves to the next stage until the document or approval from the previous stage is in the order file.
Enquiry: record who asked, what product, quantity, destination and their required documents.
Sample: send a labelled sample from a real lot, keep an identical retained sample, and get written approval.
Proforma invoice: state product, quantity, unit price, Incoterm and named place, payment terms and delivery date. Production starts only after the buyer accepts it and agreed payment has arrived.
Production: make, check, weigh and record each lot against the spec.
Documents: commercial invoice, packing list, certificates; book transport with your forwarder.
Shipment and payment: send document copies to the buyer, follow the goods, and confirm payment through your bank.
Print the SOP and stick it on the wall of your store. When a new helper joins, train them through one real order with the SOP in hand.

List the information a UK or EU prepacked food label must carry

Audit an existing label and write a corrected version

Your Nigerian label was designed for NAFDAC and local shoppers. An export label must follow the **destination country's** law. Rules differ by country and product type, so this lesson uses the UK and EU food rules as a worked model, because they are clear, published and often asked for by diaspora shops. For other destinations, ask the buyer for their rules and check official sources.
A paper tag label
The label must speak the destination's legal language, not only yours.
What a UK or EU prepacked food label must show
The **name of the food**, describing what it really is.
The **list of ingredients**, in descending order of weight.

**Allergens** from the list of 14 legally declared allergens (these include peanuts, nuts, sesame, cereals containing gluten, milk, eggs, soya, fish and crustaceans), emphasised inside the ingredients list, for example in **bold**.
The **net quantity** in metric units (g or kg) for packs above 5 g.
A **best before** or **use by** date, plus any storage conditions or instructions for use.
The **name and address of the business** responsible; your importer will usually tell you whose details must appear.
**Country of origin** where it is required, and a **nutrition declaration** for most prepacked foods.
All information in a **language** consumers in that country understand, with mandatory text at a minimum x-height of 1.2 mm (0.9 mm on packs whose largest surface is under 80 square cm).
Cosmetics are different

Shea creams, soaps and oils sold as cosmetics in the UK or EU fall under cosmetics law, not food law. They need a responsible person based in that market, a safety assessment and notification before sale. Do not ship cosmetics for retail sale there until a buyer or partner in that market has agreed to act as responsible person.
Worked example: auditing a ginger and sesame mix label for a UK shop

For example, Ada in Enugu sells a 200 g 'Ginger Pepper Mix' (ginger, sesame, chilli, salt). A London shop wants to stock it. Her current label says: 'Ginger Pepper Mix. 100% natural, no chemicals. Net Wt 200g. Best before: 6 months from production. Made in Nigeria. NAFDAC No.'
Ingredients: missing. She adds 'Ingredients: ginger, **sesame** seeds, chilli, salt' in descending weight order with sesame in bold, because sesame is one of the 14 allergens.
Date: 'six months from production' cannot be checked by a shopper. She prints an actual best before date with each lot, plus 'Store in a cool, dry place'.
Claims: 'no chemicals' is meaningless (salt is a chemical) and could mislead. She removes it.
Business details: the shop confirms the UK importer's name and address must appear; she adds it beside 'Produced in Nigeria by' her own details.
Nutrition: she asks the importer whether a nutrition declaration is needed for this product and arranges laboratory analysis if so.
She prints a test label and measures the smallest lower-case letter with a ruler to confirm it is at least 1.2 mm high.

Ada's corrected label carries ingredients with the allergen emphasised, a real date, storage advice, the importer's details and no misleading claims. She keeps the old and new versions in her export file with the importer's written approval.

Before your first shipment, run a simple **home drop test**: pack one carton exactly as you will ship it and drop it from about waist height onto a hard floor on its bottom, one corner, one edge and one side. Many first exports lose money because the price was set from the local price plus 'something'. An export price is **built up** from your real costs, then the costs of getting goods to the point where the buyer takes over, then your margin. The point where the buyer takes over is defined by an **Incoterm**.
Incoterms in plain words

**Incoterms** are rules published by the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC). The current version is **Incoterms 2020**, with 11 rules. Each rule says which tasks, costs and risks belong to the seller and which to the buyer, and where risk passes. They do not set the price or say when the buyer must pay; you agree those separately. Seven rules suit any transport mode (EXW, FCA, CPT, CIP, DAP, DPU, DDP) and four are only for sea and inland waterway (FAS, FOB, CFR, CIF).

For example, Amina in Kaduna is quoting 500 kg of dried split ginger to a UK importer. All figures are examples for practice; she uses her own records and real quotes.

The importer also asks for CIF Felixstowe. Her forwarder quotes, for example, £350 sea freight for the lot and £15 insurance: 350 / 500 = £0.70 and 15 / 500 = £0.03 per kg. CIF = 1.98 + 0.70 + 0.03 = £2.71 per kg, or £1,355 for 500 kg.

Light, bulky goods such as folded textiles and dried leaves are often charged on volume, so pack them tightly.

Finally, compare your price with what the product sells for in the destination: if the shop price there is lower than your landed cost, the market or the product needs rethinking.

For small first orders, a common compromise is a **deposit** (for example 50%) before production and the **balance** before goods are released or before shipping. Receive foreign payments into your business account through your bank, and keep the Form NXP and bank advice in the order file.
Answering an enquiry well

Reply to serious enquiries within one or two working days, in clear and polite English, from a business email address. Attach your spec sheet, a price list naming the Incoterm and place, your minimum order, your realistic monthly capacity and your standard payment terms. Ask the buyer's required documents in the same message. A complete, organised first reply sets you apart from many suppliers who answer with only a price.
Samples

Send samples from a real lot, labelled exactly as the final product, with your spec sheet and price list. Many exporters ask unknown buyers to pay the courier cost for samples; serious buyers usually agree. For example, Chioma in Aba receives a WhatsApp message: a man says he represents a 'major Canadian importer', wants 5 tonnes of dried hibiscus monthly, and asks her to send 10 kg of free samples and pay a 'supplier registration fee' to his agent.

She replies politely asking for the company's full name, registration number, website and the buyer's role, and proposes a video call.
She offers a 200 g sample from lot HB-2611-03, courier cost paid by the buyer, plus her spec sheet and a price list on FCA Lagos terms.
She states that she does not pay supplier registration fees and that first orders require a 50% deposit, with the balance before shipment.

Worked example: chargeable weight for a mixed air shipment

For example, Ngozi in Lagos ships to a buyer by air through a forwarder using a factor of 6,000. She has 6 cartons of dried ginger (each 50 x 40 x 30 cm, 14 kg) and 1 carton of adire scarves (60 x 40 x 40 cm, 6 kg).
Ginger carton volume: 50 x 40 x 30 = 60,000 cubic cm. Volumetric weight = 60,000 / 6,000 = 10 kg. Actual weight 14 kg is higher, so each is charged at 14 kg; 6 cartons = 84 kg.
Scarf carton volume: 60 x 40 x 40 = 96,000 cubic cm. Volumetric weight = 96,000 / 6,000 = 16 kg. Actual weight is only 6 kg, so it is charged at 16 kg.
Total actual weight = 84 + 6 = 90 kg. Total chargeable weight = 84 + 16 = 100 kg.
She asks whether the scarves can go in a smaller box. Folded tightly into a 40 x 30 x 30 cm carton (36,000 cubic cm), the volumetric weight is 36,000 / 6,000 = 6 kg, equal to the actual weight.
Repacking the scarves cuts the chargeable weight from 100 kg to 90 kg, saving 10 kg of freight on one shipment with no change to the goods.

Alone or together?

Some products only become exportable at volume: for example dried hibiscus or ginger by sea. If your worst-month output is far below what importers order, consider **group supply**: several producers making the same product to one shared specification, with shared lot records, checked by one quality lead and sold under one exporter's name or a registered cooperative. The agreement must be written down: who checks quality, how weights are recorded, how payment is shared, and what happens to a lot that fails the spec.

If you form a group, decide its legal form early. A registered cooperative society (registered with your state's cooperative department) or a company registered with CAC can hold the bank account, sign export contracts and be the registered exporter with NEPC. An informal group with no legal identity cannot easily do these things, and members have little protection if a payment goes wrong.
Light, high-value products such as adire, beadwork or small batches of a speciality spice can often start alone, with small air or courier shipments to diaspora shops, and grow from there.

Exporting means a buyer in another country receives your goods legally, in good condition, at a price that still pays you. A product that sells well in Ibadan may be a poor export.
So choose one product first. Then pick one market with a simple scorecard. Then check the registrations and permits you need before any foreign buyer can receive your goods.
Five tests
Can this product travel?
Fragility: glass and liquids break
Rules: food and cosmetics are strictest
Repeatable supply
Freight is charged mostly by weight. A product worth a lot per kilogram, like an adire scarf, carries freight easily.
Shipping can take weeks, so the product must stay good. Keep dated samples in final packaging and check them every month. A written record, not a guess.
Glass jars break. And food and cosmetics face the strictest rules abroad.
Last, supply. Offer a buyer the volume of your worst recent month, not your best. Failing on the second order damages trust more than a smaller honest answer.

Choosing one market
Find the code, then score the countries
Weights must add up to 100%. Easier rules get a higher score.
Find your HS code, confirm with a forwarder
Check who imports it on Trade Map
Check duties on Market Access Map
Pick four criteria and weight them
Score each country from 1 to 5, multiply
Every product crossing a border has an HS code, a customs number. Duties and paperwork depend on it, so confirm it with your forwarder. Whole and ground ginger can sit on different lines.
Free tools from the International Trade Centre help. Trade Map shows which countries import your product. Market Access Map shows duties and requirements.
Then build a weighted scorecard. Choose criteria such as demand, ease of rules, logistics cost and buyer contacts. Score each country and multiply by the weight.
Check that your weights add up to 100%. And score rules so that easier means higher, so every high number is good.

Your export base
Tick only what you actually hold
Now your Nigerian base. Register your business with CAC. Register as an exporter with NEPC. Your bank processes Form NXP, so export payments come back through the banking system.
Then find your regulator. NAQS for plant products, NAFDAC for food and cosmetics, SON for standards. Ask your buyer in writing which documents their country needs.
Protect your money
Real buyer or warning sign?
Safe practice
Verify the company
Speak by video call

Warning signs

Overpays, wants the difference back

Abroad, a missing certificate can hold goods at the port while charges grow. So check every document twice. And verify every buyer, for example on Companies House for UK firms, and speak by video call.

Real buyers do not ask suppliers to pay for their import permits. Beware of payments bigger than the invoice with a request to send back the difference. Never ship on credit to a first-time buyer you cannot verify.

Why this matters
Buyers judge you on paper first
A spec sheet says exactly what they get
A label that follows their country's law
A carton that survives the journey
A price built up from your real costs
Foreign buyers judge you on paper before they taste or touch anything. They want a written specification, and a label that follows their country's law, not only NAFDAC's.
Your carton must survive lifting, stacking and humid sheds. And your price must be built up from real costs. Many first exports lose money because the price was the local price plus something.
The spec sheet
What goes on one page
Description: form, colour, origin
Quality limits from the buyer
Packing and labelling
Storage and shelf life evidence
Documents you can supply
A specification, or spec sheet, describes exactly what the buyer will receive. It also helps your helpers make the product the same way every time.
Quality limits, such as maximum moisture, differ between buyers. Do not invent them. Copy the buyer's own numbers into your sheet.
Give every batch a lot number, print it on every bag, and keep a retained sample of each lot. If a complaint comes months later, you can check where the fault started.
Worked example
Hauwa checks ten bags from one lot
Check the lowest bag, not only the average.
Rule: no bag below 1,000 g
Weigh 10 bags picked at random
Average 1,007.4 g: looks fine
Lowest 996 g and 998 g: two fail
Raise the target to 1,010 g, recheck all
For example, Hauwa in Kano packs 1 kg bags of dried hibiscus. Her importer's rule is simple: no bag below 1,000 g. She weighs 10 bags picked from the start, middle and end of packing.
The average is 1,007.4 g, which looks fine. But one bag is 996 g and another 998 g. Two of ten break the rule.
She raises her filling target to 1,010 g, tops up every light bag, and records the change. The average alone would have hidden the problem.
Export labels
Ada fixes her label for a UK shop
Local label
No ingredients list
6 months from production
Claims 'no chemicals'
Export label
Ingredients, sesame in bold

For example, Ada in Enugu sells a 200 g ginger pepper mix. A London shop wants it. Her label has no ingredients, a date nobody can check, and the claim no chemicals, which means nothing, because salt is a chemical.
Her new label lists ingredients by weight, prints a real best before date with storage advice, and adds the UK importer's details. She checks the smallest letters are at least 1.2 mm high.
Safety and the law
Three label rules that protect people
UK and EU law names 14 allergens, such as sesame and peanuts. Emphasise them in the ingredients.
Shea creams and soaps need a responsible person in the UK or EU before retail sale.
Remove any claim you cannot prove, such as 'cures' or 'no chemicals'.
Allergens can make people seriously ill. In the UK and EU, 14 allergens must be emphasised, for example in bold. Sesame is one, so Ada puts it in bold.
Creams and soaps fall under cosmetics law there. Do not ship them for retail until a partner in that market agrees to act as responsible person.
And remove any claim you cannot prove.
Cartons
Pack to survive the journey
New double-wall carton, right size
Liner for dried foods, space filled
Tape in an H pattern, top and bottom
Drop test before your first shipment
Shipping marks match the packing list
Use new double-wall cartons sized so items cannot move. Line them for dried foods, and tape in an H pattern.
Before your first shipment, drop one packed carton from waist height on its bottom, a corner, an edge and a side. Then mark every carton, for example 1 of 6, matching your packing list exactly.
Incoterms 2020
Where your costs and risk stop
Goods ready at your premises. The buyer does everything else, even export clearance.
Handed to the buyer's carrier at a named place, export-cleared. A good first choice.
You pay sea freight and insurance, but risk passes once goods are on board.

Incoterms are rules from the International Chamber of Commerce. Each one says where your costs and risk end. Under Ex Works, the buyer does everything, which can be hard with Nigerian export formalities.
Free Carrier, F C A, is often the best first choice. Your costs stop at a place you know, such as your forwarder's warehouse.
Under CIF you pay freight to the destination port, but the risk passes at loading. Always write the rule, the named place and Incoterms 2020 on every quote.

For example, Amina in Kaduna is quoting 500 kg of dried split ginger to a UK importer.
Ginger, drying, labour, packing
Transport and documents to Lagos
Per kg. Practice figures, approximate.
Amina builds her price up from her own records, per kilogram.
Product and packing cost 2,550 naira per kg. Road transport and documents to her forwarder in Lagos add 600 per kg.
That is 3,150 naira. She adds a 20% margin, making 3,780. At an example rate of N2,000 to the pound, that is £1.89. She adds a 5% currency buffer: £1.98 per kg, FCA Lagos, valid for 14 days.
For CIF Felixstowe, she adds freight and insurance: £2.71 per kg.
Key points
Remember
Take quality limits from the buyer
Check the lowest bag weight
Label to the destination's law
Emphasise allergens, drop false claims
Build the price up, add a buffer
To remember. Take quality limits from the buyer. Check the lowest bag, not just the average. Label to the destination's law and emphasise allergens.
Build your price up from cost, name the Incoterm, and add a currency buffer and a validity period.

From product to payment
What this module covers
Find and check real buyers
Choose safe payment terms
Run the first shipment without mistakes
Plan the next 90 days
A buyer is not real until you have checked who they are and agreed how you will be paid. New exporters lose more money to poor payment terms and fake buyers than to shipping accidents.
Then you run a first shipment where every document agrees, and turn your remaining gaps into a dated plan.
Five checks before you trust anyone
Real buyers do not ask suppliers to pay fees.
Full company name, number, address, website
Check the company register in their country
Look at the email domain
Video call with practical questions
Ask for a trade reference

Meet buyers through NEPC, diaspora shops, trade fairs, or larger exporters who need more supply. Then check them. Get the full company details, and check the register. For UK companies, Companies House is free online.
A real importer rarely uses only a free email address for big orders. Hold a video call and ask which products they import and which documents their customs need. Ask for a trade reference.
Worked example
Chioma gets a suspicious enquiry
Warning signs
5 tonnes monthly, no quality questions
Wants 10 kg of free samples
Fee to be paid to his agent
Her safe reply
Asks for company details, video call
200 g sample, courier paid by buyer
No fees, 50% deposit first

For example, Chioma in Aba gets a WhatsApp message. A man says he represents a major Canadian importer, wants 5 tonnes of dried hibiscus monthly, and asks for 10 kg of free samples and a supplier registration fee.

She replies politely. She asks for company details and a video call, and offers a 200 g sample with the courier paid by the buyer. She does not pay fees, and first orders need a 50% deposit. The buyer stops replying. Chioma lost nothing.
Payment terms
From safest to riskiest for you
Cash in advance, or a deposit: safest
Letter of credit: documents must match
Documentary collection: medium risk
Open account: only for trusted buyers
Cash in advance is safest for you. A letter of credit means the buyer's bank pays if your documents match exactly, so a small spelling error can delay payment.
With documentary collection, the buyer can refuse the documents and leave goods at the port. Open account means you ship first and wait. Keep that for buyers you know and trust.
Never share your bank PIN, passwords or one-time codes with anyone. Fraudsters send fake new bank details, so confirm any change by phone on a number you already know.
Ngozi checks her chargeable weight
You pay for the higher of actual and volumetric weight.
6 ginger cartons: charged at actual 84 kg
Scarf carton: 6 kg, but 16 kg by volume
Total charged: 100 kg, not 90 kg
Smaller scarf box: 6 kg by volume
Saves 10 kg of freight

Airlines charge the higher of actual weight and volumetric weight. Ngozi's forwarder uses a factor of 6,000. Her ginger cartons are heavy, so they are charged at their actual weight. But her light scarf carton is big, so it counts as 16 kg.
So she pays for 100 kg, though the goods weigh 90. She folds the scarves tightly into a smaller box, and saves 10 kg of freight with no change to the goods.
Before cartons leave
Incoterm and place on the invoice
Copies sent to the buyer
Most first-shipment problems are small mismatches. Copy names and descriptions from one master sheet into the commercial invoice, packing list and certificates.
Give each helper a role, and have a second person check every line separately. A shortcut a local customer forgives can get goods refused at a foreign port.
Amina's 90-day budget
For example, Amina plans her first dried ginger export to Ghana from Kaduna.
Laboratory testing, weeks 5 to 7
Labels and 50 cartons, week 8
Practice shipment file
Example estimates from quotes, plus NEPC fees.

Turn every gap into an action with an owner, a target week and a cost from a real quote. Days 1 to 30 are registrations and questions. Days 31 to 60, product work. Days 61 to 90, a paid sample, a quote and a shipment file.
In week 1 Amina registers with NEPC, and in week 2 she asks the buyer and NAQS which documents Ghana needs.
She budgets about 150,000 naira for lab testing if the buyer requires it, 85,000 for labels and cartons, with her sister Hadiza as packing lead, and 20,000 for the shipment file.
That is about 255,000 naira plus NEPC fees. Every Friday she ticks off what is done. If your product needs volume, consider group supply under a written agreement.
Key points
Remember
Check every buyer before you trust them
Start with a deposit or cash in advance
Never share PINs or one-time codes
Every document must agree
Gaps become dated, costed actions
To remember. Check every buyer, and start with cash in advance or a deposit. Protect your bank codes. Make every document agree, with a second checker.
And after each shipment, ask the buyer for feedback and fix issues before you grow.
